displayQuote: There are four hundred thousand words in the English language, and there are seven you can't say on television

meta.title: Who really said "There are four hundred thousand words in the English language, and there are seven you can't say on television"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Carlin. The line comes early in "Seven Words You Can Never Say on Television" on Class Clown (1972) - not the 1973 routine at issue in the Supreme Court case.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are four hundred thousand words in the English language, and there are seven you can't say on television'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: George Carlin, Class Clown (1972), recorded 27 May 1972 in Santa Monica. The 1973 version that reached the Supreme Court does not contain this line.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Carlin states it early in “Seven Words You Can Never Say on Television,” the closing track of his album Class Clown, recorded live at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium on 27 May 1972 and released that September. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ prints this exact wording under Class Clown (1972), cited to that recording, and follows it with the ratio — “399,993 to 7.”

source.heading: The record

docMeta.dd: “Seven Words You Can Never Say on Television”
27 May 1972 — Santa Monica Civic Auditorium, Santa Monica, California

source.excerpt: Yeah, there are 400,000 words in the English language and there are 7 of them that you can’t say on television. What a ratio that is!
trail: Wikiquote’s George Carlin page ↗ prints the line among its sourced quotes under the heading “Class Clown (1972),” with a citation to the recording of 27 May 1972 — not in its Misattributed section.

A widely circulated fan transcript of the routine ↗ renders it “there are 7 of them that you can’t say on television. What a ratio that is!” with the follow-up “399,993 to 7.” It is not an authority on which take it transcribes — it mislabels the performance as the WBAI broadcast — so we defer to Wikiquote’s recording-cited wording for the quotation itself.

Wikipedia’s entry on Class Clown ↗ confirms the album was recorded 27 May 1972 at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium, released 29 September 1972 on Little David / Atlantic, and closes side two with the seven-words routine.

The 1973 rewrite is a different text: the transcript appended to FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726 ↗ — the “Filthy Words” monologue broadcast by WBAI — opens “Aruba-du, ruba-tu, ruba-tu” and contains no sentence about the number of words in the English language.
source.excerptNote: That is how a widely circulated fan transcript of the routine renders the line. Transcriptions of the delivered audio differ: Wikiquote’s sourced Class Clown section ↗, citing the 27 May 1972 recording, prints the shorter “seven you can’t say on television,” and other renderings sit in between. We have not audited the tape ourselves, so we quote Wikiquote’s recording-cited wording as the canonical form and treat the rest as approximate. Same joke, same routine either way.

author.name: George Carlin
author.heading: Who was George Carlin?
author.metaLine: 1937–2008 · American stand-up comedian, social critic & author
author.bio: Born in New York City on 12 May 1937, Carlin spent five decades turning language itself into his subject — the euphemisms, the taboos, the words institutions decide you may not use. Class Clown (1972) consolidated the shift from clean-cut TV comic to counterculture voice that FM & AM had announced that January, and it is the album that set him on the way to fourteen HBO specials. His seven-words routine put him at the centre of FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, the 1978 Supreme Court case that still shapes American broadcast indecency rules. He died in Santa Monica on 22 June 2008.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The authorship is not in doubt — this one really is Carlin. What goes wrong is the source: the line gets filed under the Supreme Court case and under the wrong album — and transcripts of the delivered wording do not quite agree with one another.

items.why: The routine that reached the Supreme Court was “Filthy Words” from Occupation: Foole (1973), broadcast by WBAI on 30 October 1973 — as Wikipedia’s account of the case sets out ↗. The verbatim transcript appended to the Court’s opinion ↗ does not contain this sentence at all. Quoting the line and citing the case cites the wrong performance.

Nobody quoting this is misattributing it, but no two transcripts of the routine agree word for word. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, cited to the 27 May 1972 recording, prints “seven you can’t say on television”; a circulating fan transcript ↗ has “7 of them that you can’t say”; other renderings drop the “that.” We have not audited the audio, so treat any word-for-word version as approximate. The substance is not in dispute.

Carlin’s list has an ancestor: in a 1966 performance Bruce said he had been arrested over nine words, a routine documented alongside Carlin’s ↗. That is a precursor to the list, not to this sentence — the four-hundred-thousand framing is Carlin’s.

Carlin is one of the internet’s most reliable false-attribution magnets — Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ strips out “The Paradox of Our Time” (written by Bob Moorehead), “I Am a Bad American,” and a drift of 1990s email one-liners. This line is not one of them; it sits in the sourced column.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Carlin’s, and it is precisely locatable: the opening of “Seven Words You Can Never Say on Television” on Class Clown, recorded 27 May 1972 ↗ — the album before the version that made it to court.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentence is doing structural work, not just being funny. By opening with a ratio — four hundred thousand against seven — Carlin reframed censorship as an arithmetic absurdity before he had named a single word. The argument is finished in the first line; everything after it is elaboration.

The framing outlived the joke. When a Pacifica station aired the 1973 rewrite, “Filthy Words,” on 30 October 1973, the resulting complaint became FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, decided 5–4 on 3 July 1978 — the case that gave American broadcast regulators their indecency authority. Carlin later said he took a perverse pride in ending up a footnote in judicial history.
context.detailsSummary: The two versions, and why the difference matters
detailsBody: 1972 — “Seven Words You Can Never Say on Television,” Class Clown. Recorded 27 May 1972 at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium; released 29 September 1972 on Little David / Atlantic. This is the version that contains the four-hundred-thousand line.

1973 — “Filthy Words,” Occupation: Foole. A reworking of the same material. This is the one WBAI broadcast on 30 October 1973 and the one transcribed in full as an appendix to the Supreme Court’s opinion. Its text differs throughout — it opens “Aruba-du, ruba-tu, ruba-tu” — and the ratio line is absent from it entirely.

Because the second version is the one preserved in a court record, it is the easiest to find and the easiest to cite — which is exactly how a line from the first album ends up footnoted to the second.
context.pull: 399,993 to 7. They must really be bad.
